Nelson Mandela: President of South Africa from 1994 to 1999.
Known as 'Light of the Faith,' this Zengid dynasty ruler governed Seljuk Syria from 1146 to 1174 and looms large in the history of the Second Crusade — who was he?
Nur al-Din Zengi: Emir of Aleppo (1146–1174) and Damascus (1154–1174)
The first prime minister of India from the south, he steered the country's 1991 economic liberalisation after previously serving as chief minister of Andhra Pradesh — who is he?
P. V. Narasimha Rao: Prime Minister of India from 1991 to 1996.
A four-star general who staged a 1999 coup against Nawaz Sharif's government, this military officer went on to serve as Pakistan's president from 2001 to 2008 — who was he?

Pervez Musharraf: President of Pakistan from 2001 to 2008. Pervez Musharraf (11 August 1943 – 5 February 2023) was a Pakistani politician and military officer who served as the tenth president of Pakistan from 2001 to 2008.
This act of deliberate communication with a deity — through hymns, incantations, or spontaneous words — has been documented in written sources for some five thousand years — what is it called?
Prayer: Invocation or act that seeks to activate a rapport with a deity.

Serving as India's president from 2017 to 2022, he was the first person from Uttar Pradesh and the first member of the Bharatiya Janata Party to hold that office, after serving as Governor of Bihar — who is he?
Ram Nath Kovind: President of India from 2017 to 2022.

Fought from 1921 to 1926, this conflict pitted Spain and later France against Berber guerrillas led by Abd el-Krim in northern Morocco, and saw history's first amphibious landing to use tanks and aircraft — which conflict?
Rif War: 1921–1926 war between Spain and Riffian tribes of Morocco.
Founded by a Varangian prince who settled at Novgorod in 862, this noble lineage ruled Kievan Rus' and, through its Moscow branch, the tsars of Russia until 1598 — what dynasty was it?
Rurikids: Noble lineage and rulers of Kievan Rus'. The Rurikids were the ruling dynasty of Kievan Rus' and its principalities following its disintegration.
After leaving office, she traded the Finnish prime minister's chair for a desk at the Tony Blair Institute, advising on leadership reform — which young Social Democrat was she?
Sanna Marin: Prime Minister of Finland from 2019 to 2023.
Serving as Argentina's Minister of Economy from 2022 to 2023, this politician had earlier been Chief of Cabinet under Cristina Fernández de Kirchner and twice mayor of Tigre — who is he?
Sergio Massa: Argentine politician and lawyer (born 1972)
A media tycoon worth $6.8 billion at his death, which Italian served as prime minister across three separate governments between 1994 and 2011?
Silvio Berlusconi: Italian media tycoon and politician (1936–2023)
The first Louisianian to serve as House majority whip since the early 1970s, he has represented Louisiana's 1st congressional district since 2008 — who is he?

Emphasizing harmony with an enigmatic guiding force behind reality, this Chinese philosophical and religious tradition promotes effortless action, simplicity, and the three treasures of compassion, frugality, and humility — which tradition?
Taoism: Religious and philosophical tradition. Taoism or Daoism is a philosophical and religious tradition indigenous to China, emphasizing harmony with the Tao 道.
Cao Wei, Shu Han and Eastern Wu carved up China between 220 and 280 AD after the collapse of the Han dynasty — what is this era called?
Three Kingdoms: Period of Chinese history from 220 to 280 CE.

Political theorist Roger Griffin traced this extreme, supremacist strain of national pride — an ideological foundation beneath Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany — to the view of nations as living organisms with 'great cultural destinies.' What's it called?
A two-time Chief Minister of Maharashtra who also served as India's Minister of Earth Sciences, this Indian National Congress politician hailed from the Latur district — who is he?
A rags-to-riches Western Han general celebrated for his campaigns against the Xiongnu, he rose through ties to Emperor Wu and was uncle to the famed general Huo Qubing — who was he?
After serving as a concubine and then empress, this woman founded her own short-lived Zhou dynasty to become the only undisputed female sovereign in China's history — who was she?
Wu Zetian: Empress regnant of China from 690 to 705.
Revered as the Father of the Nation, this ruler of Abu Dhabi became the first president of a newly unified Gulf federation in 1971?
Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan: President of the United Arab Emirates from 1971 to 2004.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Levi Strauss (born 1829) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was established earliest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these was founded earliest?
MUMPS (founded 1966) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is an astronomer?
John Flamsteed is an astronomer. John Flamsteed (19 August 1646 – 31 December 1719) was an English astronomer and the first Astronomer Royal.
Which of these is a mathematician?
Grigori Perelman is a mathematician. The full details of Perelman's work were filled in and explained by various authors over the following several years.
What is the atomic number of Radon?
Radon is a chemical element; it has symbol Rn and atomic number 86.
What is the atomic number of Gallium?
Gallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ga and atomic number 31.
In what year was Edward Witten born?
Edward Witten: Witten is a researcher in string theory, quantum gravity, supersymmetric quantum field theories, and other areas of mathematical physics.
In what year was Milton Friedman born?
Milton Friedman: Friedman's challenges to what he called "naive Keynesian theory" began with his interpretation of consumption, which tracks how consumers spend.
In what year was Karl Marx born?
Karl Marx: Born in Trier in the Kingdom of Prussia, Marx earned a doctoral degree in philosophy from the University of Jena in 1841.
In what year did Alexander Graham Bell die?
Alexander Graham Bell: Bell considered his invention an intrusion on his real work as a scientist and refused to have a telephone in his study.
In what year did Max Planck die?
Max Planck: Max Karl Ernst Ludwig Planck (German: [ˈmaks ˈplaŋk]; 23 April 1858 – 4 October 1947) was a German theoretical physicist.
In what year was Boron discovered?
Boron is a chemical element; it has symbol B and atomic number 5.
Dopamine: Pfizer. Dopamine (DA, a contraction of 3,4-dihydroxyphenethylamine) is a neuromodulatory molecule that plays several important roles in cells.
In which country is TAI TF Kaan?
TAI TF Kaan: Turkey. Designed to replace the Turkish Air Force’s fleet of F-16 Fighting Falcons, the Kaan is also intended for export to international markets.
Who is credited with discovering Leo Minor?
Leo Minor: Johannes Hevelius. Leo Minor is a small and faint constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere.
Who is credited with discovering Graph theory?
Graph theory: Leonhard Euler. In mathematics and computer science, graph theory is the study of graphs, which are mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects.
Who is credited with discovering Budesonide?
Budesonide: Ralph Brattsand. Budesonide, sold under the brand name Pulmicort, among others, is a steroid medication.
Who is credited with discovering Platinum?
Platinum: Julius Caesar Scaliger. Platinum is a chemical element; it has symbol Pt and atomic number 78.
These large seabirds of the tubenose order range widely across the Southern Ocean and North Pacific, but are notably absent from the North Atlantic today. What birds are they?
Albatross are large seabirds related to the procellariids, storm petrels, and diving petrels in the order Procellariiformes (the tubenoses).
One of Ptolemy's original 48 and among the largest in the sky, this autumn constellation is named for a mythical princess chained to a rock for the sea monster Cetus — which one?
Andromeda (constellation) is one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century Greco-Roman astronomer Ptolemy, and one of the 88 modern constellations.
Named from the Ancient Greek word for silver, this condition results from too much silver exposure and can leave the skin permanently blue-gray — what is it?
Argyria is a condition caused by excessive exposure to chemical compounds of the element silver, or silver dust.

Manufactured by a Turkish company and credited largely to a former MIT graduate, this medium-altitude combat drone has become one of the most exported unmanned aircraft of its era — what aircraft (family) is it?
Baykar Bayraktar TB2 is a family of medium-altitude long-endurance (MALE) unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAV) capable of remotely controlled or autonomous flight operations.
Native to cool parts of Europe and Asia, this deciduous shrub produces small, glossy black berries especially rich in vitamin C and vulnerable to cold snaps during spring flowering — name the fruit?
Blackcurrant (Ribes nigrum), black currant or cassis is a deciduous shrub in the family Grossulariaceae grown for its edible berries.

Forced to flee Italy in 1938 under the racial laws, this experimental physicist had earlier invented an improved coincidence circuit and traveled to Eritrea to show cosmic rays arrived more strongly from the West than the East — who was he?
Bruno Rossi (13 April 1905 - 21 November 1993) was an Italian-American experimental physicist.
A child prodigy who became director of the Göttingen Observatory, this German polymath left his mark on number theory, algebra, geometry, statistics, and probability alike — who is he?
Carl Friedrich Gauss (30 April 1777 - 23 February 1855) was a German mathematician, astronomer, geodesist, and physicist, who contributed to many fields in mathematics and science.
Atomic number 17, this strongly oxidising yellow-green gas sits between fluorine and bromine on the periodic table — what element is it?
Chlorine is a chemical element; it has symbol Cl and atomic number 17.
This bird group's rock-dove species gave rise to most domesticated pigeon breeds, including racing and fantail pigeons, and was later introduced to the Americas — which classification is it?
Columba (genus) comprises a genus of medium to large pigeons.
This actor known for eccentric roles broke out playing a teenager's awkward father in a 1985 time-travel classic. Who is he?
Crow is a bird of the genus Corvus, or more broadly, a synonym for all of Corvus.
Its genus name translates to 'two-crested lizard,' honoring the twin head-crests found on fossils unearthed in Arizona in the 1940s — which Early Jurassic predator is this?
Dilophosaurus (dy-, -foh-) is a genus of theropod dinosaurs that lived in what is now North America during the Early Jurassic, about 186 million years ago.

Specializing in legislative process and authoritarian rule, this Russian scholar became a fellow at a Berlin academy and hosts her own political radio talk show, reaching a million YouTube subscribers by 2022 — who is she?
Ekaterina Schulmann (ne Zaslavskaya; born 19 August 1978) is a Russian political scientist specializing in legislative processes and authoritarian governance.
This flammable, colorless solvent smells sweetly of pear drops and shows up in glues and nail polish remover — and it's also the ester used to gently strip caffeine from tea and coffee. What is it?
Ethyl acetate (commonly abbreviated EtOAc or EA) is the organic compound with the formula CH3CO2CH2CH3, simplified to C4H8O2.
Using a skin membrane called a patagium plus a long tail for steering, these gliding rodents can sail from tree to tree without true flight — what are they called?
Flying squirrel (scientifically known as Pteromyini or Petauristini) are a tribe of 50 species of squirrels in the family Sciuridae.
Arriving late to a lecture, this mathematician copied down two famous unsolved problems thinking they were homework — and solved them; he's better known for the simplex algorithm, but who was he?

George Dantzig (November 8, 1914 - May 13, 2005) was an American mathematical scientist who made contributions to industrial engineering, operations research, computer science, economics and statistics.

These common coastal seabirds, most closely related to terns and skimmers, were once known by an older name still surviving in some English dialects and cognate with the German word Möwe — what birds are they?
Gull (see Taxonomy), are seabirds of the subfamily Larinae.
First identified in 1910, this organic compound is stored in mast cells and basophils and, though not made by classic endocrine glands, still acts as a local hormone — what compound is it?
Histamine is an organic nitrogenous compound found in mammals and many vegetables, fruits and food products.

This phenomenon describes how a system's state depends on its history, as when a magnet holds different moments depending on past field changes — it underlies memory in a hard disk drive. What is it called?
Hysteresis is the dependence of the state of a system on its history. Hysteresis can be found in physics, chemistry, engineering, biology, and economics.

This English mathematician made foundational contributions to matrix and invariant theory, founded the American Journal of Mathematics at Johns Hopkins, and was teaching at Oxford when he died. Who was he?
James Joseph Sylvester (3 September 1814 - 15 March 1897) was an English mathematician.
This Indian aerospace engineer served as secretary of the Department of Space and chairman of both ISRO and the Space Commission — who is he?
K. Sivan (born 14 April 1957) is an Indian aerospace engineer who served as the secretary of the Department of Space and chairman of ISRO and Space Commission.
The last member of the actinide series, this synthetic element is named for the inventor of the cyclotron — which element holds atomic number 103?
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lr (formerly Lw) and atomic number 103.

Built by an American defense contractor with partners including Northrop Grumman and BAE Systems, this single-engine, single-seat stealth fighter comes in conventional, short-takeoff, and carrier-launched variants — name the aircraft?
Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II is an American family of single-seat, single-engine, supersonic stealth strike fighters.
An economist by training, he became the only Sikh to lead India and the first prime minister since Nehru to be re-appointed after a full five-year term — who is he?
Manmohan Singh (26 September 1932 - 26 December 2024) was an Indian economist, bureaucrat, academician and statesman who served as the prime minister of India from 2004 to 2014.
This field of study examines and evaluates the procedures researchers use to gather and interpret data, rather than the findings those procedures produce — what is it called?
Methodology is the study of research methods.
Sitting just above the lip and under the nose, this style of facial hair on men has come in countless shapes across the centuries — what's it called?
Moustache is a growth of facial hair grown above the upper lip and under the nose of men.
This form of vitamin B3 is taken orally to treat pellagra without the skin-flushing side effect of niacin, and used as a cream to fight acne and reduce signs of aging skin — what's the compound?
Nicotinamide (INN, BAN UK) or niacinamide (USAN US) (IUPAC name: 3-pyridinecarboxoamide) is a form of vitamin B3 found in food and used as a dietary supplement and medication.
These red-haired great apes once roamed all of Southeast Asia but now cling to just Borneo and Sumatra — and in 2017 scientists confirmed a brand-new third species among them. Which animal is it?
Orangutan are great apes native to the rainforests of Indonesia and Malaysia.

One of the 20th century's most prolific mathematicians, this Hungarian championed Ramsey theory — the study of when order must inevitably appear — and cracked countless open problems across number theory and combinatorics; who was he?
Paul Erdős (26 March 1913 - 20 September 1996) was a Hungarian mathematician known as one of the most prolific mathematicians and producers of mathematical conjectures of the 20th century.

This branch of linguistics studies how languages organize their foundational sound units — like the contrast between 'bat' and 'gnat' — or, in sign languages, elements like hand shape and location — what is it called?
Phonology (formerly also phonemics or phonematics) is the branch of linguistics that concerns how languages organize the foundational elements that make their words.

Native to most of the Northern Hemisphere, this genus of 25 to 30 deciduous tree species includes poplars, aspens, and cottonwoods, one of which was the first tree ever fully DNA-sequenced — which genus?
Populus is a genus of 25-30 species of deciduous flowering plants in the family Salicaceae, native to most of the Northern Hemisphere.

Brought from China to Europe in the sixteenth century and popularized by the House of Orange in the Netherlands, this dog breed is known for its wrinkly, short-muzzled face and curled tail — name the breed?
Pug is a breed of dog with the physically distinctive features of a wrinkly, short-muzzled face, and curled tail.
Which large Southern African dog breed, whose standard was drafted in 1922 in what's now Zimbabwe, descends from ridged hunting dogs of the Khoikhoi crossed with European breeds used to bay lions?
Rhodesian Ridgeback is a large dog breed originally bred in Southern Africa.
Once placed in its own plant family before molecular studies folded it into Dracaena, this African and Asian succulent genus includes the plant nicknamed 'devil's tongue' — which genus?

Sansevieria is a historically recognized genus of flowering plants, native to Africa, notably Madagascar, and southern Asia, now included in the genus Dracaena on the basis of molecular phylogenetic studies.

Dubbed the "father of modern differential geometry," this Chinese-born American mathematician and poet won the Wolf Prize — and has a medal named for him by the International Mathematical Union. Who was he?
Shiing-Shen Chern (pinyin: Chn Xngshn; October 26, 1911 - December 3, 2004) was a Chinese-born American mathematician and poet.

Meaning 'pore bearer' in Greek, this phylum of sessile, filter-feeding marine invertebrates has tube-like bodies of jelly-like material sandwiched between thin cell layers, letting water circulate through countless pores — name the animal group?
Sponge are primarily marine invertebrates of the animal phylum Porifera (meaning 'pore bearer').

In the nervous system, this structure lets one neuron send or receive signals with a neighboring cell, and comes in both chemical and electrical varieties — the electrical kind linked directly through gap junctions — name this structure?
Synapse is a structure that allows a neuron to exchange (receive or send) signals with another cell in its immediate vicinity.
A European Space Agency astronaut who is also a musician and writer, this Frenchman logged two six-month stints aboard the ISS, the second launched via SpaceX Crew Dragon in 2021 — who is he?
Thomas Pesquet (French; born 27 February 1978, is a French aerospace engineer, pilot, European Space Agency astronaut, actor, musician, and writer.
Built in the Soviet Union from 1966 to 1989 for short-haul routes, this narrow-body jet earned the NATO codename 'Crusty' — which airliner is it?
Tupolev Tu-134 (NATO reporting name: Crusty) is a twin-engined, narrow-body jet airliner built in the Soviet Union for short and medium-haul routes from 1966 to 1989.
Named from a French verb meaning 'to see,' this term describes the practice of secretly watching others in intimate moments, often labeled 'Peeping Tom' behavior — what is it?
Voyeurism is the habit of clandestine watching other people engaged in intimate behaviors, such as undressing, sexual activity, or other actions of a private nature, commonly for sexual stimulation.

Native to freshwater and brackish habitats across western Eurasia, this ray-finned fish in the perch family, related to perch, ruffe, and darters, has become a popular game species well beyond its original range. Name it?
Zander (Sander lucioperca), sander or pikeperch, is a species of ray-finned fish from the family Percidae (which also includes perch, ruffe and darter).
Marked by inadequate cortisol and aldosterone production in the adrenal glands, this rare, long-term endocrine disorder is also known as primary adrenal insufficiency — what is it?
Addison's disease: Endocrine disorder. Addison's disease arises when the adrenal gland does not produce sufficient amounts of the steroid hormones cortisol and (sometimes) aldosterone.
His mother and wife were both deaf, which steered this Scottish-born inventor toward hearing devices — and, in 1876, the first U.S. patent for the telephone. Who was he?
Alexander Graham Bell: Inventor of the telephone (1847–1922)
This inorganic salt, most commonly used as a soil fertilizer, is 21% nitrogen and 24% sulfur by content — what is it?
Useless against the cold, the flu, or any fungus, this kind of medicine works only by killing or stalling bacteria — what is it called?
Antibiotic: Antimicrobial substance active against bacteria.

This umbrella term for joint disease covers conditions like osteoarthritis, most common in weight-bearing joints as people age, and the autoimmune form that typically targets the hands and feet. What condition is this?
This Indian jurist studied economics at Columbia and the London School of Economics before becoming the chief architect of his country's constitution. Who was he?
B. R. Ambedkar: Indian jurist, economist, politician and social reformer (1891–1956)
Originating in the Swiss Alps' canton of Bern, this large farm breed historically pulled carts for alpine herders and traces its ancestry to Roman mastiffs — which breed, recognized in 1912?
Bernese Mountain Dog: Swiss breed of dog. The Bernese Mountain Dog, German: Berner Sennenhund or Dürrbächler, is a large dog breed originating from the canton of Bern, Switzerland and the Swiss Alps.
The only trijet ever produced by its manufacturer, this airliner entered service with Eastern Air Lines in 1964 powered by three rear-mounted turbofans?
Ranging from roughly seawater-strength up to a fully saturated 26%, which salty solution is used for pickling food, de-icing roads, and turns up as a wastewater byproduct of desalination?
Brine: Concentrated solution of salt in water.
Named for the Latin word for the first day of the month, this daisy-family genus is commonly called marigold and is prized in herbal and cosmetic products — which plant?
Calendula: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.
Its Greek-derived genus name Xylocopa literally means 'wood-cutter,' fitting for an insect that burrows nesting tunnels into dead wood or bamboo — which insect is it?
Carpenter bee: Common name for a genus of bees.

Serving as royal executioner under Louis XVI and later chief executioner of the First Republic, this Frenchman carried out nearly 3,000 executions during his 40-year career, including those of the king, queen, and Robespierre — who is he?

Also bearing the names Krebs and TCA, this loop of biochemical reactions unlocks the energy in nutrients via the oxidation of acetyl-CoA — and is thought to be one of the earliest metabolic components. What is it?
Citric acid cycle: Interconnected biochemical reactions releasing energy.
In this prolonged state of deep unconsciousness, a person cannot be awakened, shows no normal sleep-wake cycle, and may even be induced deliberately during general anesthesia — what is it?
Coma: State of unconsciousness. The person may experience respiratory and circulatory problems due to the body's inability to maintain normal bodily functions.
First described in 1880 by a French neurologist, this rare delusion convinces sufferers that they are dead, don't exist, or have lost their internal organs — what is it called?
Cotard's syndrome: Delusion that one is dead or non-existent.
Bred in Germany with short legs and a long body to chase badgers into their burrows, which hound breed comes in smooth-, wire-, and long-haired varieties?
Sold as Voltaren and taken by mouth, suppository, injection, skin gel, or even eye drops, this NSAID eases pain and inflammation like gout for up to eight hours a dose — what is it?
Revered by Ancient Egyptians as the god Khepri for rolling the sun across the sky, which insect feeds exclusively on feces?
Dung beetle: Informal group of insects.
Born in Pretoria and once a Zip2 co-founder, this CEO of Tesla and SpaceX became, by some estimates, the first dollar trillionaire in 2026 — who is he?
Elon Musk: Businessman and public official (born 1971)
Also called moral philosophy, this field splits into normative, applied, and meta- branches as it asks what people ought to do and whether objective moral facts even exist. Which discipline is it?
Nicknamed the "Warthog" and flying since 1977, this straight-winged, twin-turbofan attack jet is the only U.S. production aircraft built solely for close air support against tanks — what is it?

Fairchild Republic A-10 Thunderbolt II: American close air support attack aircraft. In service since 1977, it is named after the Republic P-47 Thunderbolt strike-fighter of World War II, but is commonly referred to as the "Warthog".
Grown for both food and fiber, this plant's seeds are pressed into linseed oil while its stem fibers are woven into linen for sheets and clothing. What plant is it?

After dropping out of Harvard to help build early versions of Windows at Microsoft, this developer co-founded a studio that made Half-Life and later launched a digital storefront called Steam — who is he?

Caused by excess growth hormone before a child's growth plates fuse — usually from a pituitary tumor — this rare disorder produces height at least three standard deviations above average. What condition is it?
Gigantism: Human growth disorder. It is a rare disorder resulting from increased levels of growth hormone before the fusion of the growth plate which usually occurs at some point soon after puberty.
One of the heaviest snakes alive, which non-venomous constrictor prefers shallow, slow-moving South American waters like flooded grasslands and rivers?
An English GP convicted in 2000 of murdering 15 patients, he's reckoned one of history's most prolific serial killers with an estimated 250 victims — who was he?
Harold Shipman: English doctor and serial killer (1946–2004)
The offspring of a stallion and a female donkey, this equine hybrid is the rarer reciprocal cross to the mule and was often mistaken in European folklore for a horse-cow hybrid — what is it?
Hinny: Domestic horse–donkey hybrid. It is the reciprocal cross to the more common mule, which is the product of a male donkey (a jack) and a female horse (a mare).
First made in Belgium in 1956 and sold under the brand names Atarax and Vistaril, this first-generation antihistamine also treats anxiety and insomnia — what drug?
Hydroxyzine: Antihistamine drug. It is used in the treatment of itchiness, anxiety, insomnia, and nausea (including that due to motion sickness).

According to psychologist Alfred Adler, this persistent feeling of being deficient or lesser than others — often stemming from childhood comparisons to a sibling — can lead people to overcompensate. What is it called?
Inferiority complex: Intense feeling of inadequacy and inferior.
This Canadian-American physical educator invented a global team sport, wrote its original rule book, and founded the University of Kansas's program for it in 1898 — who is he?

An Alberta-born clinical psychologist and University of Toronto professor, he drew huge attention in the late 2010s for his cultural and political views — self-identifying as a classical liberal. Who is he?

Also called 47,XXY, this chromosome anomaly leaves those affected phenotypically male but often infertile, and is named after the American endocrinologist who first identified it in the 1940s — what's the condition?
Formulated in 1834, this principle of electromagnetism states that an induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the very change in magnetic field that created it — which principle?
Lenz's law: Electromagnetic opposition to change.

Providing the USAF with intercontinental strategic airlift for oversized cargo, this jumbo transport is among the largest military aircraft ever built and shares lineage with the smaller Starlifter — what is it?
Lockheed C-5 Galaxy: American heavy military transport aircraft.
This marsupial family native to Australia and New Guinea includes kangaroos, wallabies, and the quokka among its 63 recognized species — what is it?
Macropodidae: Family of marsupial mammals. Macropodidae is a family of marsupials that includes kangaroos, wallabies, tree-kangaroos, wallaroos, pademelons, the quokka, and several other groups.

Captured by Einstein's famous equation E=mc², this principle shows that a tiny amount of one physical quantity converts into an enormous amount of another thanks to the speed of light being squared — what is this relationship called?
Mass–energy equivalence: Physics concept expressed as E = mc².
Aristotle called it the 'first philosophy' — the branch that probes existence itself, what all things have in common, and how reality is divided into categories of being. Which field is it?
Normally equal to 60 seconds, which unit of time has occasionally run 61 seconds long in UTC due to leap seconds, though a 59-second version has never actually occurred?
Minute: Unit of time equal to 60 seconds. The prime symbol ′ is also sometimes used informally to denote minutes.
Sold under the brand name Bactroban, this topical antibiotic treats impetigo and clears MRSA from the nose — what is it?
Derived from the Greek word for kidney, this medical specialty covers kidney function, disease, and treatments ranging from diet changes to dialysis and transplantation — which field?
Nephrology: Medical study concerned with the kidneys.
Built from nucleotide units — a sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base — this biomolecule class includes both DNA and RNA. Which class of molecule?
Nucleic acid: Class of large biomolecules essential to all known life.
Nicknamed the fish hawk, this diurnal bird of prey has a wingspan up to 180 centimeters and hunts almost exclusively fish — which bird?
Osprey: Species of bird. The osprey (Pandion haliaetus), historically known as sea hawk, river hawk, and fish hawk, is a diurnal, fish-eating bird of prey with a cosmopolitan range.

First described by a 17th-century French mathematician in 1653, this fluid mechanics principle states that a pressure change at any point in a confined, incompressible fluid is felt equally throughout it — what's it called?
Pascal's law: Principle in fluid mechanics. The law was established by French mathematician Blaise Pascal in 1653 and published in 1663.
Called the 'father of transplantation,' this Brazilian-born biologist won a 1960 Nobel for his work on acquired immune tolerance and graft rejection — who was he?

Cultivated for its edible nuts since prehistoric times and native to the Mediterranean and the Levant, this pine species has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit — which species?
Pinus pinea: Species of pine tree. Pinus pinea, the Italian stone pine or Mediterranean stone pine, is a tree from the pine family, Pinaceae.
Stockpiled for radiation emergencies, this oral compound floods and shields the thyroid gland — and also treats hyperthyroidism and the skin infection sporotrichosis. Which compound is it?

Harvested from Plantago seeds mainly grown in northern India, this dietary fiber relieves both constipation and mild diarrhea, and can modestly lower cholesterol and blood pressure with regular use. What is it?
Psyllium: Plant used as a dietary fiber.
This genus of muroid rodents gives its scientific name to the common rat, though not every animal called a rat actually belongs to it — which genus?
Sold under the brand name Rituxan, this monoclonal antibody treats non-Hodgkin lymphoma, rheumatoid arthritis and several other autoimmune conditions via slow IV infusion — what is it?
Named after a 19th-century American veterinary surgeon, this genus of rod-shaped, flagella-covered bacteria includes over 2,650 serotypes divided among just two species — what is it?
Salmonella: Genus of bacteria. Salmonella is a genus of rod-shaped, (bacillus) Gram-negative bacteria of the family Enterobacteriaceae.
This class of central nervous system depressant increases GABA activity to calm irritability and anxiety, distinct from drugs used mainly to induce sleep — what is it?
Sedative: Drug that reduces excitement without inducing sleep.
In this rare congenital condition affecting about 1 in 10,000 people, the heart and other major organs sit as a mirror image of their normal position — what's it called?
Situs inversus: Condition in which organs are reversed.

Made of a segmented series of bones cushioned by intervertebral discs, this defining feature of some 50,000 animal species surrounds and protects the nerve tissue running through it — what is it, also known as the backbone?
Spinal column: Bony structure found in vertebrates.

This small nocturnal marsupial has membranes stretching from its forelegs to hindlegs that let it soar between trees, and its scientific name translates to 'short-headed rope-dancer' — what animal is it?
Sugar glider: Species of Australian marsupial.
A staple from the Caribbean to Oceania to East Asia, this Araceae-family plant is prized for the starchy underground corm it grows much like a yam — what is it?
Taro: Species of plant. Taro (Colocasia esculenta) is a root vegetable.
This English economist and cleric argued in an 1798 essay that population growth would always outpace food production gains, dooming society to hardship — who is he?
